# Expanding Our Pre-Bid Dataset Using Aerospike and Kafka


[DV Engineering](https://medium.com/@dv-engineering?source=post_page---byline--8756895c7dbc-----------------------------------------)


6 min read


·


Just now


--


*Written By:*[Jason Reed](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jason-reed-541a467b/?lipi=urn%3Ali%3Apage%3Ad_flagship3_profile_view_base%3BU2%2BSPIIbRfiInqME96Q8Tg%3D%3D)


At DV, our pre-bid service is called during real-time bidding — the high-speed auctions used to sell ad impressions across web and app environments. The service handles hundreds of billions of requests per day and must respond in milliseconds. It performs complex business logic and consults dozens of datasets to determine whether the auctioned ad placement meets our client advertisers’ standards.


Historically, we met these requirements by pre-loading copies of each dataset into each service instance’s memory. When a new version of one of our largest datasets grew from 30 million to over 200 million records, we decided to explore a new approach, moving beyond local in-memory replication to a more centralized, highly scalable datastore.


This post covers how we stored that dataset in Aerospike, scaled ingestion with Apache Kafka, tuned the Aerospike client and replicated globally, while meeting strict freshness and latency targets.


## Expanding Beyond Local Memory


With the arrival of this new, large dataset, storing the data in a high-performance datastore like Aerospike promised several benefits. Aerospike is designed for sharding, distributed replication and persistence on SSD, providing a highly available, durable and scalable solution. Aerospike clusters are built to support a large volume of lookups at low latency; other teams at DV had experienced consistent sub-millisecond performance on high-volume workloads.


Using a centralized datastore provided some simplicity and efficiency benefits as well. Instead of keeping hundreds of local dataset copies up to date, we could focus on one shared Aerospike cluster per region. New service instances would no longer have to wait the additional minutes to load the full dataset before serving requests. We worked with DV’s platform team to set up and start loading our data into some test Aerospike clusters.

## Streaming Data Into Aerospike


The new 200 million record dataset was produced to a Kafka topic by an upstream team. Around 50 million Kafka messages were written to the topic per day, in batches. We targeted data availability within minutes, so we wanted a solution that could process large message volumes quickly.


To load from Kafka to Aerospike, we used the Aerospike Connect inbound Kafka connector, which is built on the Kafka Connect framework. In addition to data loading, the connector allows users to configure simple functions (single-message transforms, or SMTs) to transform data before writing it to Aerospike. We used a combination of built-in and custom SMTs to format our data efficiently, filter it, and set record-level TTLs.


We set up the connector and began to test it on the full production-scale dataset. During extended testing of the data loading component, we saw unpredictable spikes in the incoming message rate that caused the connector to build up a Kafka lag that wasn’t cleared fast enough to meet our data freshness targets. Fortunately, the source topic was sufficiently partitioned, and Aerospike Connect can scale out seamlessly, distributing tasks and Kafka partitions across multiple instances. We scaled out and quickly had a solution capable of handling the peak workload.


## Optimizing Aerospike Lookup Performance


Next, our service had to start retrieving data from Aerospike. Consistent low latency was critical to meeting our performance targets. We used Aerospike’s Java client library to do key-value lookups. In our first pass, we tried using asynchronous lookups. We ran load tests to simulate real request volume and noticed that under high load, P99 Aerospike client latency was surprisingly high, reaching several milliseconds. Aerospike’s internal latency was very fast, suggesting the additional latency originated outside the database. We decided to dig deeper to optimize performance to a level we could release in production.


We tested multiple Aerospike client approaches and configurations. We tried both synchronous and asynchronous Aerospike clients, using varied workloads to simulate handling our real-world request load of tens of thousands of requests per second per service instance. We adjusted client settings, such as the maximum number of concurrent in-flight requests and the event loop configurations used by the asynchronous client.


After several rounds of testing, we decided to go with synchronous lookups. Under our tested workloads, synchronous lookups showed lower CPU usage and had more consistent tail latency than the asynchronous configurations we evaluated. Synchronous lookups were also simpler to integrate into the service code.


Once we had a performant client configuration, we began using Aerospike in production. We gradually rolled out the new data to partner integrations in our first region. After verifying performance, we were ready to launch our Aerospike dataset globally.

## Replicating Aerospike Across Regions


DV operates in a number of regions. We host our pre-bid service in each of these regions near our partners to provide quick responses. With the new cache system, we needed to set up Aerospike locally in each region to stay fast.


Our platform team provisioned Aerospike clusters in each region. We ingested the data into one regional Aerospike cluster, then replicated it to other regions using Aerospike’s cross-datacenter replication (XDR). We enabled Aerospike in each region one by one, with our service instances using nearby Aerospike clusters. Replication worked smoothly, and we were able to roll out Aerospike usage worldwide.

## Monitoring and Observability


For this first wide rollout of Aerospike usage, monitoring was crucial to catch issues rapidly and keep our service performing reliably. We took advantage of Aerospike’s built-in monitoring capabilities and implemented additional client-side monitoring. We monitor the data-loading process, the Aerospike DB clusters and the Aerospike lookups in our service. We have separate dashboards and sets of alerts for each of these three major components.


Some key metrics we monitor from the data-loading process include:


- Kafka message arrival rate
- Kafka lag
- Connector read/write rate
- Connector timeout/exception rate
- Connector task status
- Number of records in Aerospike
- Time from Kafka message creation to Aerospike write
- Rate, lag, and errors in cross-datacenter replication


To track the performance of lookups from our service, we observe:


- Hit/Miss rate
- Client timeouts/exceptions
- Aerospike DB lookup latency
- Client round-trip lookup latency


Our platform team owns the monitoring of the Aerospike DB itself. They provide views into key DB-internal metrics, including available storage capacity, hardware resource usage, replication and partitioning.


## Production Performance


Over several months, we’ve rolled out Aerospike and our expanded dataset across regions and integrations. Right now, the pre-bid service performs over 20 billion Aerospike lookups per day with consistent sub-millisecond round-trip latency. We write around 40 million records per day to our new cache and meet our latency and data-freshness needs.


Operationally, Aerospike has been remarkably smooth to work with. It helps to have a battle-tested platform team watching over the infrastructure! Our service no longer has to load this large dataset, and we’ve seen significant improvements in startup time. The large, frequently updating dataset we migrated is now more scalable and easy to manage.


## Building on Our Aerospike Foundation


Following the success of our first large Aerospike dataset migration, we moved additional datasets to Aerospike, including several of the pre-bid service’s largest. We introduced near caching for datasets that change less frequently, and we refined our data preprocessing. Together, these improvements simplified operations, reduced startup times, and improved the elasticity and scalability of our pre-bid service.
